introduction_markdown:
**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Subject: Religious Studies (code 0785), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2022. Paper 2: The Old Testament/Jewish Bible and World Faiths. Duration: three hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Answer FOUR questions chosen from any ONE SECTION ONLY. All questions carry equal marks (25 marks each).

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

Sections of the paper: 1.0 The Old Testament/Jewish Bible, Section 1.1 The Patriarchs to David (questions 1 to 6); Section 5.3 Islam (questions 7 to 12); Section 5.5 African Traditional Religious Beliefs and Practices (questions 13 to 18).

À faire relire par un spécialiste des études religieuses avant mise en avant.

questions.enonce_markdown: Examine Jacob as an incarnation of conflicts. (25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** To call Jacob "an incarnation of conflicts" is to say that his life, from before birth to old age, was marked by struggle with other people and with God. The accounts in Genesis 25 to 50 support this claim, although they also show how the struggles were turned into blessing.

**1. Conflict before birth and in childhood.** The twins Jacob and Esau struggled in Rebekah's womb (Genesis 25). Jacob was born holding Esau's heel, and the name Jacob is linked with "heel" or "supplanter". The oracle announced that the older would serve the younger, so the rivalry was part of his identity from the beginning.

**2. Conflict with Esau.** The conflict grew when Jacob obtained Esau's birthright for a meal of stew (Genesis 25), and then, with the help of his mother, the blessing of Isaac by deception (Genesis 27). Esau decided to kill him, and Jacob had to flee.

**3. Conflict within the family.** The parents were divided: Isaac loved Esau, Rebekah loved Jacob. Later Jacob's own household was torn between his wives Leah and Rachel, who competed through children and their maids (Genesis 29 and 30), and his favouritism towards Joseph caused the brothers' hatred and the sale of Joseph into Egypt (Genesis 37).

**4. Conflict with Laban.** In Haran Jacob, the deceiver, was himself deceived when Laban gave him Leah in place of Rachel (Genesis 29). Over twenty years there were disputes over wages and flocks, and a tense departure, with Laban chasing him and a covenant made at Mizpah (Genesis 31).

**5. Inner and spiritual conflict.** Jacob feared Esau's revenge and prayed for deliverance (Genesis 32). At the ford of the Jabbok he wrestled with a mysterious man until daybreak, was wounded in the hip and was renamed Israel, "he who strives with God" (Genesis 32). This was the climax of a struggle with God and with his own past.

**6. Conflict with the neighbours.** The rape of Dinah and the revenge of Simeon and Levi at Shechem placed Jacob in conflict with the Canaanites (Genesis 34), and he rebuked his sons.

**7. Resolution.** The conflicts did not end in destruction. Jacob and Esau were reconciled (Genesis 33), Joseph forgave his brothers (Genesis 45 and 50) and Jacob blessed his sons. The name Israel became the name of the nation.

**Conclusion.** Jacob's life was deeply marked by conflicts with his brother, parents, father-in-law, wives, sons and God, and the claim is largely true. Genesis however shows that God worked through these conflicts: they shaped Jacob from supplanter into Israel, father of the twelve tribes.
